Question: Why is it that the C programming language can be used across multiple different devices but Assembly cannot?
Old_Answer: I assume you mean “multiple different architectures” as opposed to “multiple different devices.” We're long past the days when each computer was unique by about 75 years, give or take. Assembly language isn't one language. Rather, it's the human readable form of the machine code for a particular processor architecture family. Each family has its own instruction set. There may be many different mutually incompatible dialects of assembly code for the same instruction set. For example, look up MASM and AT&T syntax for x86 assembly code. The Z80 is largely backward compatible with the 8080; however, because Intel® copyrighted* their instruction set, Zilog developed their own mnemonics and syntax. (*It’s unclear whether that copyright claim was meaningful.) In fact, you can even have incompatibility within the same assembly language dialect for the same processor family. Newer family members may support instructions and registers that aren't present on older family members, for instance. Instructions for newer processors won't work on older processors that lack those extensions. Now, there have been some assembly translators. It works best when the architectures involved are related, and the newer one takes translation into account. 8080 → 8086 is a famous example. These translators are rare. C code, on the other hand, can be compiled for whatever target architectures the compiler supports. As long as you stick to certain rules and build the right abstractions, it's not that difficult to write portable C code. All you need is a compiler for whatever target architecture you're interested in, and in many cases you are in good shape. It does take effort and care. It's orders of magnitude more approachable than porting large piles of assembly language though. Addendum Since it came up in discussion on a different answer, I figured I would mention it here. If you run the assembled code in a simulator or interpreter, then you can run your assembly language wherever you’ve ported the simulator/interpreter. That assembly language can even target a virtual machine, rather than a real CPU. That particular thread brought up EFI byte code specifically. My answer focuses on assembly code for the native instruction set in its native form. That's what I believe most people think of when they see that phrase without further qualifications. You can develop other kinds of assembly language with different properties. For example, you could create an assembly language that provides a common subset of core operations and abstract “registers,” and use macros or a specialized tool to generate the actual machine code for different machines. Or you could create an assembly language that targets various sorts of virtual machines, such as JVM byte code, CPython byte code, EFI byte code, UCSD pCode, Microsoft’s pCode, etc. When describing it to others, you should call out the fact that it's not traditional native assembly language, otherwise you're likely to cause confusion.

Consequently, what works in one assembly language for a particular processor, like x86, may not translate or even run on another, such as ARM or MIPS, due to differences in how these CPUs are designed to process instructions and manage memory. Thus, the unique characteristics of each machine’s architecture necessitate that assembly languages remain inherently machine-dependent, making them powerful tools for optimization but also limiting their portability across different systems. In summary, the linkage between assembly language and machine architecture is fundamental, ensuring that each assembly language is tailored to its specific hardware environment.
